title: Views, triggers, and stored routines

spans.text: “Views, triggers, and stored routines” is a tool for solving a concrete programming problem. Identify the input and desired result, then trace what role the construct plays in the example. Study it not only as syntax, but also for its effects on readability, correctness, resource use, and future changes.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
When a price changes, the trigger records the old and new values in price_audit.

A VIEW is a named SELECT query, not a separate copy of the data. A trigger runs automatically after an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE and can enforce rules such as writing an audit record. Stored procedures and functions keep program logic in the database; PostgreSQL and MySQL support them with different languages and syntax. SQLite supports triggers but does not provide a server-style stored procedure system. Assign ownership of each rule clearly instead of duplicating it in both the application and a trigger.

Key line: `CREATE TABLE price_audit (`
What it does: When a price changes, the trigger records the old and new values in price_audit.
Why it is used: Document trigger side effects and possible trigger chains; verify changes with migrations and tests.
If omitted or changed: Stored-procedure syntax is not portable between PostgreSQL and MySQL; the example here demonstrates SQLite trigger syntax only.
